What frequency do channel loss specifications quote, and why?
column2: The Nyquist frequency, half the symbol rate: the fundamental of an alternating pattern, the highest frequency the receiver must recover with full amplitude. A 212.5 Gb/s PAM4 lane runs 106.25 GBd, so its Nyquist is 53.125 GHz.

column1: How do conductor and dielectric loss scale with frequency?
column2: Conductor (skin-effect) loss grows as \(\sqrt f\); dielectric loss grows as \(f\). Dielectric loss therefore dominates at high frequency in ordinary laminates.

column1: What is the dielectric loss of a line?
column2: \(\alpha_d = \pi f\sqrt{\varepsilon_r}\tan\delta/c\) Np/m, about \(2.3f_{GHz}\tan\delta\sqrt{\varepsilon_r}\) dB/in. It comes from \(G'Z_0/2\) with \(G' = \omega C'\tan\delta\).

column1: What is the smooth-copper conductor-loss rule of thumb?
column2: \(\alpha_c \approx 36\sqrt{f_{GHz}}/(w_{mil}Z_0)\) dB/in, multiplied by a roughness factor \(K_r = 1 + (2/\pi)\arctan[1.4(\Delta_{rms}/\delta)^2]\).

column1: What is copper's skin depth at 1 GHz?
column2: About 2.09 µm (0.52 µm at 16 GHz). Surface roughness comparable to the skin depth raises the loss.

column1: Where does a via stub notch the channel?
column2: At its quarter-wave frequency \(c/(4\ell_{stub}\sqrt{\varepsilon_r})\). Back-drilling shortens the stub to push the notch well above Nyquist.

column1: What sets near-end crosstalk (NEXT)?
column2: A plateau of height \(K_bV_a\) with \(K_b = \tfrac14(C_m/C + L_m/L)\), lasting twice the coupled delay; it saturates for coupled lengths beyond \(vt_r/2\).

column1: Why is far-end crosstalk zero in homogeneous stripline?
column2: FEXT is proportional to \(C_m/C - L_m/L\); in a homogeneous dielectric the capacitive and inductive ratios are equal and cancel. In microstrip they do not.

column1: What is ground bounce?
column2: \(V \approx L_{ret}N\Delta I/t_r\): N drivers switching together through a shared return inductance.

column1: What is a PDN's target impedance?
column2: \(Z_{target} = \Delta V/\Delta I\): the allowed ripple divided by the transient current, to be held across the frequencies the load excites.

column1: What loss budget does PCIe 6.0 allow?
column2: 32 dB at 16 GHz (PCIe 5.0: 36 dB at 16 GHz).

column1: What is the peak-distortion eye height for NRZ and PAM-M?
column2: NRZ: \(h_0 - \sum_{k\ne0}|h_k|\). PAM-M: \(h_0/(M - 1) - \sum_{k\ne0}|h_k|\), so PAM4's eyes are a third as tall for the same ISI.

column1: How does BER depend on eye height?
column2: \(\text{BER} = Q(V_{eye}/2\sigma)\) for NRZ and \(\tfrac34Q(V_{eye}/2\sigma)\) for Gray-coded PAM4.

column1: What are \(Q^{-1}\) at 10⁻⁶, 10⁻¹² and 10⁻¹⁵?
column2: 4.75, 7.03 and 7.94. A 1.5× drop in eye height can take a link from 10⁻¹² to 10⁻⁶.

column1: What is total jitter in the dual-Dirac model?
column2: \(TJ(\text{BER}) = 2Q^{-1}(\text{BER})\,RJ + DJ(\delta\delta)\); at 10⁻¹² the multiplier is 14.07. Eye width is \(UI - TJ\).

column1: What does a bathtub curve show, and what is a Q-scale plot?
column2: BER against sampling position; its width at a BER is the eye width. On a Q-scale (\(Q^{-1}\) of BER) each wall is a straight line, which makes extrapolation easy.

column1: What is a first-order CDR's jitter tolerance?
column2: \(A_{tol}(f) = M\sqrt{1 + (f_c/f)^2}\): it tracks slow jitter (large tolerance below the loop bandwidth) and rejects only the margin \(M\) at high frequency.

column1: How long must a zero-error BER test run?
column2: About \(3/\text{BER}\) bits for 95% confidence (the rule of three).

column1: Why do modern links specify pre-FEC error targets?
column2: Links run with FEC; PCIe 6.0 and 7.0 target a first-bit error rate of 10⁻⁶ before FEC, and Ethernet's KP4 FEC tolerates about 2.4 × 10⁻⁴.

column1: What is COM?
column2: Channel operating margin: \(20\log_{10}(A_s/A_{ni})\) dB, signal over noise and interference at the target error rate for a reference receiver; 3 dB is the usual pass threshold.

column1: How does interleaving relax a SerDes clock?
column2: With N-way interleaving the clock runs at \(f_{baud}/N\) with phases 360°/N apart, each one UI.

column1: CML or voltage-mode (SST) driver: which uses less power and why?
column2: SST: \(P = V_{reg}^2/200\ \Omega\) against CML's \(V_{DD}V_{pp,diff}/50\ \Omega\), about 4:1 for the same swing and supply, because CML burns its tail current continuously.

column1: How does a transmit FFE combine with the channel?
column2: The received cursors are \(g_k = \sum_jc_jh_{k-j}\); under a peak-swing limit \(\sum|c_j| = 1\), so equalizing costs low-frequency amplitude.

column1: What is a source-degenerated CTLE's peaking?
column2: \(H(\infty)/H(0) = 1 + g_mR_S/2\), with a zero at \(1/(R_SC_S)\) and a pole at \((1 + g_mR_S/2)/(R_SC_S)\). It equalizes mostly by losing DC gain.

column1: Why must a DFE's first tap close in one UI?
column2: The decision on symbol n−1 must be fed back before symbol n is sliced: \(t_{clk-q} + t_{settle} + t_{setup} < 1\) UI. Loop unrolling (speculation) relaxes it at the cost of comparators.

column1: Why does a DFE not amplify noise?
column2: It subtracts ISI using past decisions, not the noisy signal, unlike a linear equalizer's high-frequency boost.

column1: What is DFE error propagation?
column2: A wrong decision adds ISI instead of removing it: \(P(e_n|e_{n-1}) = \tfrac12Q((h_0 - 2h_1)/\sigma) + \tfrac12Q((h_0 + 2h_1)/\sigma)\), up to 0.25 when \(h_1 = h_0/2\). Errors come in bursts.

column1: How does sign-sign LMS adapt a DFE tap?
column2: \(b_k\) moves by a step in the direction of \(\text{sgn}(e_n)\,\text{sgn}(\hat a_{n-k})\); it converges when residual ISI from symbol n−k is zero.

column1: What phase error does a first-order CDR show under frequency offset?
column2: \(\Delta f_{baud}/(2\pi f_c)\) UI: wider loop bandwidth reduces it but passes more jitter.

column1: When does PAM4 beat NRZ on a lossy channel?
column2: When the extra loss NRZ suffers at its doubled Nyquist exceeds PAM4's 9.54 dB eye penalty: \(L > 9.54/[\alpha(\sqrt2 - 1) + 1 - \alpha]\) dB, 9.5–23 dB from dielectric- to conductor-dominated channels.

column1: Why did long-reach SerDes move to ADC-and-DSP receivers?
column2: At 100+ Gb/s per lane the equalization needed (long FFEs, MLSD) is cheaper and more flexible in digital logic that scales with CMOS than in analog circuits.

column1: What limits an ADC's SNR through clock jitter?
column2: \(\text{SNR} = -20\log_{10}(2\pi f\sigma_t)\): 35.6 dB at 26.56 GHz with 100 fs rms. ENOB = (SNR − 1.76)/6.02.

column1: How are SerDes ADCs built?
column2: 6–7 bits, time-interleaved 64- to 128-way; slice mismatch (skew, gain, offset) must be calibrated, and skew acts like jitter.

column1: What does MLSD gain over a DFE on \(h = (1, \alpha)\)?
column2: \(10\log_{10}(1 + \alpha^2)\) dB, up to 3 dB at α = 1: it uses the energy in the post-cursor instead of cancelling it.

column1: What is net coding gain?
What does 802.3dj add for 200 Gb/s optical lanes?
column2: A concatenated inner code (8 parity bits per 120) under the RS(544,514) outer code, raising the lane to 113.4375 GBd and tolerating an inner input BER of about 4.85 × 10⁻³.

column1: What does RS(544,514) cost in latency on a 100 G lane?
column2: About 151 ns (51 ns to receive a codeword plus about 100 ns of decoding in one implementation).

column1: How does PCIe 6.0 keep FEC latency low?
column2: A light FEC on 256-byte flits (under 10 ns transmit plus receive) backed by link-level retry, rather than strong always-on FEC.

column1: How much of a DSP SerDes's power is DSP?
column2: About half in one 128 Gb/s example (4.1 against 1.89 pJ/b), which is why removing the DSP (LPO) is attractive.

column1: How do you compute a link's bandwidth?
column2: \(B = NR\eta/8\) bytes/s: lanes × rate × encoding efficiency.

column1: What are PCIe's encoding efficiencies?
column2: 8b/10b 80% (Gen 1–2); 128b/130b 98.5% (Gen 3–5); 256-byte flits with 236 bytes for TLPs (Gen 6–7).

column1: Why are small packets inefficient?
column2: Each TLP carries fixed overhead: \(\eta = P/(P + H)\); with 24 bytes of overhead a 64-byte payload is 73% efficient, 256 bytes 91%.

column1: How big must a credit or retry buffer be?
column2: At least bandwidth × round-trip time, so buffers grow with both rate and reach.

column1: What does CXL add to PCIe?
column2: Memory semantics (CXL.mem and CXL.cache) on PCIe wires: memory expansion and pooling; a x16 link at 64 GT/s carries more than two DDR5-6400 channels' bandwidth, at the cost of added latency.

column1: What is the lane rate of a 200 Gb/s Ethernet lane?
How many hosts does a two-tier leaf-spine of radix-k switches serve?
column2: \(k^2/2\) non-blocking: 2,048 at radix 64, 131,072 at radix 512.

column1: What is PCIe's cadence?
column2: Doubling the I/O bandwidth about every three years (26% a year): 64 GT/s (6.0), 128 GT/s (7.0), 256 GT/s targeted for 8.0 in 2028.

column1: What are UALink and Ultra Ethernet?
column2: UALink 200G 1.0 (April 2025): an open scale-up fabric of 200 Gb/s links to 1,024 accelerators. Ultra Ethernet 1.0 (June 2025): an Ethernet-based scale-out transport for AI and HPC.

column1: What is the energy per bit of a short unterminated wire?
column2: \(CV^2/4\) for random data: tens of femtojoules for package wires.

column1: What is the energy per bit of a terminated link?
column2: \(V^2/(4Rf_b)\): termination burns static current every bit, which is why short wires stay unterminated.

column1: How does bump pitch set areal bandwidth density?
column2: \(D = \phi r/(8p^2)\): density goes as the inverse square of pitch, so hybrid bonding wins even at low per-wire rates.

column1: What is a wire's Elmore delay?
column2: About \(R_{on}C_{tot} + R_w(C_w/2 + C_L)\), with a 10–90% rise of about 2.2 times that; often the driver, not the wire, dominates.

column1: What are UCIe's energy targets?
column2: 0.5 pJ/b (standard package), 0.25 (advanced) and under 0.05 (3D at 9 µm); UCIe 3.0 (Aug 2025) adds 48 and 64 GT/s.

column1: How does HBM4 reach 2 TB/s per stack?
column2: 2,048 data wires at 8 Gb/s each: wide and slow over short unterminated interposer wires.

column1: What does NVLink 5 give each Blackwell GPU?
column2: 18 links of 100 GB/s, 1.8 TB/s in both directions.

column1: What is the energy-per-bit ladder?
column2: From UCIe-3D (under 0.05 pJ/b) and UCIe-A (0.25) through UCIe-S and BoW (0.25–1), NVLink-class links (about 1.3, a 2023 vendor claim) and long-reach SerDes (2–3 analog) to pluggable optics (about 20): the farther a bit goes, the more it costs.

column1: Why do datacenter optics use 850 nm multimode and 1310 nm single-mode fiber?
column2: 850 nm VCSELs are cheap but multimode fiber's modal bandwidth limits reach to about 100 m; at 1310 nm single-mode fiber has near-zero dispersion, so short- and medium-reach links avoid dispersion penalties.

column1: What are G.652.D fiber's loss and dispersion?
column2: Cabled ≤ 0.36 dB/km at 1310 nm and ≤ 0.22 at 1550 nm; dispersion ≤ 3.5 ps/(nm·km) over 1285–1330 nm and ≤ 18 at 1550 nm.

column1: What is fiber latency?
column2: \(n_g/c\) ≈ 4.9 µs/km, about 5 ns per metre: at cluster scale distance, not electronics, sets the latency floor.

column1: How does dispersion spread scale with symbol rate?
column2: Spectral width \(\lambda^2\Delta f/c\) grows with rate and the UI shrinks, so spread in UI grows as the square of the rate.

column1: What is a photodiode's responsivity?
column2: \(\mathcal R = \eta q\lambda/(hc)\): ideal 0.69, 1.06 and 1.25 A/W at 850, 1310 and 1550 nm.

column1: What is the Mach–Zehnder transfer function?
column2: \(P_{out} = P_{in}\cos^2(\Delta\phi/2)\) with \(\Delta\phi = \pi V/V_\pi\); bias at quadrature. A half-Vπ swing gives 7.7 dB of extinction.

column1: What does \(V_\pi L\) tell you?
column2: Modulator efficiency: silicon depletion ≈ 2 V·cm, so a 2 V Vπ needs a centimetre; thin-film lithium niobate is also ≈ 2 V·cm with very low loss.

column1: Why do ring modulators need heaters?
column2: Their resonance shifts \(\lambda\Delta n/n_g\), about 0.056 nm/K in silicon, against a linewidth \(\lambda/Q\) of about 0.13 nm: a few kelvin detune them.

column1: What is a direct-detection receiver's sensitivity?
column2: \(P = Q\sigma/\mathcal R\) for OOK, plus \(10\log_{10}3\) = 4.77 dB for PAM4 and \(10\log_{10}[(ER + 1)/(ER - 1)]\) for finite extinction ratio.

column1: Why is PAM4's penalty 4.77 dB in optics but 9.54 dB in copper?
column2: Photocurrent is proportional to optical power, so a 3× smaller eye is 3× less optical power (4.77 dB); in copper it is 3× less voltage, 9× less power (9.54 dB).

column1: What are a shunt-feedback TIA's gain and bandwidth?
column2: \(Z_T = R_FA/(1 + A)\) and \(f_{3dB} = (1 + A)/(2\pi R_FC_{in})\); the feedback resistor adds \(\sqrt{4kT/R_F}\) of noise current.

column1: How do you convert between wavelength and frequency spacing?
column2: \(\Delta f = c\Delta\lambda/\lambda^2\): CWDM's 20 nm is about 3.5 THz at 1310 nm; DWDM's 100 GHz is 0.8 nm at 1550 nm.

column1: Why can silicon guide 1310 nm light but not detect it?
column2: Silicon's 1.12 eV gap cuts off at 1107 nm, so 1310 and 1550 nm photons pass without absorption. Germanium (direct transition ≈ 0.80 eV) detects them.

column1: Why can't silicon lase?
column2: Its band gap is indirect: radiative recombination needs a phonon and is slow, so lasers come from III-V materials (external, flip-chip or heterogeneously bonded).

column1: What does high index contrast buy and cost?
column2: Silicon in oxide (3.48 vs 1.44, critical angle 24.4°) confines light into sub-micrometre waveguides with tight bends, but its tiny mode couples poorly to a 9.2 µm fiber mode.

column1: What is the single-mode condition for a slab waveguide?
column2: \(d < \lambda/(2\sqrt{n_1^2 - n_2^2})\): about 245 nm for silicon in oxide at 1550 nm.

column1: How efficiently do two Gaussian modes couple?
column2: \(\eta = [2w_1w_2/(w_1^2 + w_2^2)]^2\), times \(\exp[-2d^2/(w_1^2 + w_2^2)]\) for offset d. A 0.5 µm mode into a 4.6 µm fiber mode couples 4.6% (−13.4 dB).

column1: Edge coupler or grating coupler?
column2: Edge couplers (spot-size converters) are broadband and polarization-tolerant but only at a diced edge; grating couplers sit anywhere and allow wafer test but steer about 0.1°/nm, limiting bandwidth.

column1: What sets a grating coupler's period?
column2: Phase matching: \(\Lambda = \lambda/(n_{eff} - \sin\theta)\); its beam steers by \(1/(\Lambda\cos\theta)\) rad per unit wavelength.

column1: Why does a 1 nH wire bond trouble a 20 fF ring modulator?
column2: With a 50 Ω driver it resonates at 35.6 GHz with ζ = 0.11 (13 dB of peaking), inside a 113 GBd lane's band; a hybrid bond's few picohenries leave the response flat to about 200 GHz.

column1: What does an MZM biased at quadrature cost in average power?
column2: 3.01 dB: the output averages half the peak transmission, before any insertion loss.

column1: What does a retimed transceiver's DSP do?
column2: Terminates the host channel (SerDes), equalizes the optical channel, retimes at each boundary so segments are budgeted separately, and handles FEC.

column1: How do impairments accumulate in retimed and linear links?
column2: Retimed: BERs add. Linear: noise adds, \(1/Q^2 = \sum 1/Q_i^2\). Three segments good for 10⁻¹² give 3 × 10⁻¹² retimed but 2.4 × 10⁻⁵ linear.

column1: What do 800G and 1.6T pluggables dissipate?
column2: NVIDIA's twin-port 800G DR4: 16 W typical; 1.6T: 33.5 W maximum. Both about 20 pJ/bit.

column1: Why does wafer-level optical test pay?
column2: Yield compounds (\(y^n\)); testing first means only good PICs collect assembly cost: \(c_P/Y + c_A\) instead of \((c_P + c_A)/Y\).

column1: What are LPO and LRO?
column2: Linear pluggable optics remove the module DSP; the host SerDes equalizes the whole link. Linear receive optics keep the transmit DSP and make only the receive path linear, for roughly half the savings.

column1: Why is LPO harder at 200 Gb/s per lane?
column2: Each segment's Q falls and linear chains add \(1/Q^2\), so the margin left above the FEC threshold shrinks; initial 1.6T LPO needed over 30 W against below 20 W for LRO.

column1: What is co-packaged optics?
column2: Optical engines on the switch package, a few millimetres from the ASIC: the electrical path drops from about 22 dB to about 4 dB at 200 Gb/s, and the module DSP disappears.

column1: What does 22 dB to 4 dB mean?
column2: 18 dB, a factor of 63.1 in power and 7.94 in amplitude: NVIDIA's '63x signal integrity'.

column1: How have Broadcom's CPO generations scaled?
column2: About 6.4 W (Humboldt), 5.5 W (Bailly) and 3.5 W (Davisson) per 800G port, against 16–18 W for pluggables: 8.0, 6.9 and 4.4 pJ/bit.

column1: What is an ELSFP?
column2: OIF's field-replaceable front-panel external laser module (11 to 26 dBm per wavelength per core) that feeds co-packaged engines over fiber; one source can feed several lanes.

column1: What does a zero-failure test of T device-hours prove?
column2: A 95% upper bound on failure rate of \(-\ln(0.05)/T \approx 3/T\): one million hours bounds it only to about 3,000 FIT; 100 FIT needs 30 million.

column1: What is blast radius?
column2: The ports one failure removes: one for a pluggable, every port of an engine for CPO. Port-hours lost scale with failure rate × ports lost × repair time.

column1: Why convert 'watts per port' to pJ/bit?
column2: Port speeds differ (800 Gb/s or 1.6 Tb/s); 25 W per port is 15.6 pJ/bit at 1.6 Tb/s but 31 at 800 Gb/s.

column1: How does CPO change the optics industry?
column2: Optics become part of the switch package and bill of materials: value shifts to the switch vendor, its foundry and laser suppliers, and operators lose the ability to mix and replace pluggables.

column1: What did Marvell pay for Celestial AI?
column2: About $3.25 B upfront ($1.0 B cash plus shares) with up to $2.25 B more in revenue-contingent shares; closed February 2026.
